claim: Serum and monocytes from patients with CF exhibit an enhanced NLRP3-inflammasome signature with increased IL-18, IL-1β, caspase-1 activity and ASC speck release.
source: Previously, we showed that serum and monocytes from patients with CF exhibit an enhanced NLRP3-inflammasome signature with increased IL-18, IL-1β, caspase-1 activity and ASC speck release (Scambler et al. eLife 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Scambler et al. eLife 2019)

claim: CFTR modulators down regulate the exaggerated proinflammatory response following LPS/ATP stimulation.
source: Here we show that CFTR modulators down regulate this exaggerated proinflammatory response following LPS/ATP stimulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: In vitro application of ivacaftor/lumacaftor to CF monocytes showed a significant reduction in IL-18.
source: In vitro application of ivacaftor/lumacaftor or ivacaftor/tezacaftor to CF monocytes showed a significant reduction in IL-18, whereas IL-1β was only reduced with ivacaftor/tezacaftor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: In vitro application of ivacaftor/tezacaftor to CF monocytes showed a significant reduction in IL-18.
source: In vitro application of ivacaftor/lumacaftor or ivacaftor/tezacaftor to CF monocytes showed a significant reduction in IL-18, whereas IL-1β was only reduced with ivacaftor/tezacaftor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: IL-1β was only reduced with ivacaftor/tezacaftor in CF monocytes in vitro.
source: In vitro application of ivacaftor/lumacaftor or ivacaftor/tezacaftor to CF monocytes showed a significant reduction in IL-18, whereas IL-1β was only reduced with ivacaftor/tezacaftor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1D

claim: Serum IL-18 decreased significantly with ivacaftor/lumacaftor treatment over three months.
source: Serum IL-18 and TNF decreased significantly with treatments, but IL-1β only declined following ivacaftor/tezacaftor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Serum TNF decreased significantly with ivacaftor/lumacaftor treatment over three months.
source: Serum IL-18 and TNF decreased significantly with treatments, but IL-1β only declined following ivacaftor/tezacaftor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Serum IL-18 decreased significantly with ivacaftor/tezacaftor treatment over three months.
source: Serum IL-18 and TNF decreased significantly with treatments, but IL-1β only declined following ivacaftor/tezacaftor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Serum TNF decreased significantly with ivacaftor/tezacaftor treatment over three months.
source: Serum IL-18 and TNF decreased significantly with treatments, but IL-1β only declined following ivacaftor/tezacaftor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Serum IL-1β only declined following ivacaftor/tezacaftor treatment.
source: Serum IL-18 and TNF decreased significantly with treatments, but IL-1β only declined following ivacaftor/tezacaftor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2F

claim: IL-18 was significantly decreased in LPS/ATP-stimulated PBMCs with both ivacaftor/lumacaftor and ivacaftor/tezacaftor combinations.
source: In (LPS/ATP-stimulated) PBMCs, IL-18/TNF/caspase-1 were all significantly decreased and IL-10 was increased with both combinations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3F

claim: TNF was significantly decreased in LPS/ATP-stimulated PBMCs with both ivacaftor/lumacaftor and ivacaftor/tezacaftor combinations.
source: In (LPS/ATP-stimulated) PBMCs, IL-18/TNF/caspase-1 were all significantly decreased and IL-10 was increased with both combinations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3H

claim: Caspase-1 was significantly decreased in LPS/ATP-stimulated PBMCs with both ivacaftor/lumacaftor and ivacaftor/tezacaftor combinations.
source: In (LPS/ATP-stimulated) PBMCs, IL-18/TNF/caspase-1 were all significantly decreased and IL-10 was increased with both combinations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4D

claim: IL-10 was increased in LPS/ATP-stimulated PBMCs with both ivacaftor/lumacaftor and ivacaftor/tezacaftor combinations.
source: In (LPS/ATP-stimulated) PBMCs, IL-18/TNF/caspase-1 were all significantly decreased and IL-10 was increased with both combinations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3J

claim: Ivacaftor/tezacaftor alone showed a significant reduction in IL-1β in LPS/ATP-stimulated PBMCs.
source: Ivacaftor/tezacaftor alone showed a significant reduction in IL-1β and pro-IL-1β mRNA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Ivacaftor/tezacaftor alone showed a significant reduction in pro-IL-1β mRNA.
source: Ivacaftor/tezacaftor alone showed a significant reduction in IL-1β and pro-IL-1β mRNA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: CFTR modulator combinations have potent anti-inflammatory properties in addition to their ability to stimulate CFTR function.
source: This study demonstrates that these CFTR modulator combinations have potent anti-inflammatory properties, in addition to their ability to stimulate CFTR function, which could contribute to improved clinical outcomes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: CFTR modulator anti-inflammatory properties could contribute to improved clinical outcomes.
source: This study demonstrates that these CFTR modulator combinations have potent anti-inflammatory properties, in addition to their ability to stimulate CFTR function, which could contribute to improved clinical outcomes.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential clinical implications

claim: Cystic fibrosis is characterised by repeated pulmonary infections and disordered innate immune-driven inflammation.
source: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is characterised by repeated pulmonary infections and disordered innate immune-driven inflammation.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about CF

claim: The NLRP3-inflammasome is a key regulator of inflammation in CF.
source: We and others have recently provided evidence supporting the hypothesis that the NLRP3-inflammasome is a key regulator of inflammation in CF (McElvaney et al., 2019; Peckham et al., 2017; Scambler et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: CF epithelia and monocytes/serum from patients with CF exhibit an enhanced pro-inflammatory signature when compared with healthy controls and patients with non-CF bronchiectasis.
source: We've demonstrated that both CF epithelia and monocytes/serum from patients with CF exhibit an enhanced pro-inflammatory signature when compared with healthy controls and patients with non-CF bronchiectasis.
evidence: Supported by prior work from the authors

claim: CF-specific increases in IL-18, IL-1β, caspase-1 activity, and ASC-speck release were all reversed by pre-treatment with epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and NLRP3-inflammasome inhibitors.
source: We observed CF-specific increases in IL-18, IL-1β, caspase-1 activity, in addition to ASC-speck release, that were all reversed by pre-treatment with epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and NLRP3-inflammasome inhibitors (Peckham et al., 2017; Scambler et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: CFTR modulators are known to correct CFTR dysfunction and partially restore CFTR-mediated ENaC inhibitory activity.
source: These small molecules are known to correct CFTR dysfunction and partially restore CFTR-mediated ENaC inhibitory activity (Cholon et al., 2014; Pranke et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The NLRP3-inflammasome senses multiple damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
source: The NLRP3-inflammasome senses multiple damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is a major component of the outer membrane of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and members of the Burkholderia cepacia complex.
source: Amongst the latter, lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is a major component of the outer membrane of two of the main pathogens found in CF airways, the gram-negative bacteriae such a Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) and members of the Burkholderia cepacia complex (B. cenocepacia).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Burkholderia cenocepacia can trigger the NLRP3-inflammasome and exacerbate the proinflammatory response through inflammasome activation and IL-1β/IL-18 processing.
source: It has been reported that the latter organism can trigger the NLRP3-inflammasome and exacerbate the proinflammatory response, both through inflammasome activation and IL-1β/IL-18 processing (Rimessi et al., 2015; Gavrilin et al., 2012; Rosales-Reyes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: In both murine and human CF, NLRP3 activity contributes to IL-1β-dependent inflammation which can be negatively regulated by anakinra, an IL-1 receptor antagonist.
source: In this regard, in both murine and human CF, NLRP3 activity contributes to IL-1β-dependent inflammation which can be negatively regulated by anakinra, an IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) (McElvaney et al., 2019; Iannitti et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: In mice, the NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 reduces IL-1β levels in the lungs, decreases airway inflammation and improves airway clearance of P. aeruginosa.
source: In mice, the NLRP3 inhibitor, MCC950, reduces IL-1β levels in the lungs, decreases airway inflammation and improves airway clearance of P. aeruginosa (McElvaney et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Defective CFTR expression and function appears to be driving inflammation by lowering the threshold of innate immune defences and reducing the ability of myeloid cells to resolve infection and inflammation.
source: Thus, defective CFTR expression and function appears to be driving inflammation, by lowering the threshold of innate immune defences and reducing the ability of myeloid cells, such as neutrophils and macrophages to resolve infection and inflammation (Barnaby et al., 2018; Bonfield et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Conditional inactivation of Cftr in myeloid cells of mice resulted in a dysfunctional immune response, with Cftr-lacking mice taking longer to resolve inflammation and to rectify infection compared to wild-type mice.
source: Conditional inactivation of Cftr in myeloid cells of mice resulted in a dysfunctional immune response, with Cftr-lacking mice taking longer to resolve inflammation and to rectify infection, when compared to wild-type (WT) mice (Bonfield et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: In young children with CF, inflammation can be detected in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid in the absence of infection, and this process is mainly driven via NLRP3-inflammasome activation.
source: Finally, in young children with CF, inflammation can be detected in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, in the absence of infection, and this process is mainly driven via NLRP3-inflammasome activation (Rosenow et al., 2019; McElvaney et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The introduction of CFTR modulators into clinical practice has resulted in a paradigm shift in therapeutic options, whereby targeting the clinico-pathogenic origin of the defective CFTR rather than the secondary effects of CFTR dysfunction has become a reality.
source: The introduction of CFTR modulators into clinical practice has resulted in a paradigm shift in therapeutic options, whereby targeting the clinico-pathogenic origin of the defective CFTR rather than the secondary effects of CFTR dysfunction has become a reality (VX17-445-103 Trial Group et al., 2019; VX17-445-102 Study Group et al., 2019; VX08-770-102 Study Group et al., 2011; Taylor-Cousar et al., 2017; TRAFFIC Study Group et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple clinical trials

claim: There are limited data on whether CFTR modulators can directly modulate CF-related inflammation.
source: These drug regimens were primarily developed to improve cell-surface expression and function of the CFTR anion channel but there are limited data on whether they can directly modulate CF-related inflammation (Barnaby et al., 2018; Hisert et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: Treatment of primary bronchial epithelial cell cultures bearing two Phe508del mutations with ivacaftor/lumacaftor depresses CXCL8 transcription, p38 MAPK phosphorylation and reduces serum levels of several proinflammatory cytokines in response to P. aeruginosa.
source: Treatment of primary bronchial epithelial cell cultures (BECs), bearing two Phe508del mutations, with the combination of ivacaftor/lumacaftor (IVA/LUM) depresses CXCL8 transcription, p38 MAPK phosphorylation and reduces serum levels of several proinflammatory cytokines, in response to P. aeruginosa (Barnaby et al., 2018; Ruffin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Treatment with ivacaftor has been reported to reduce sputum levels of neutrophil elastase, IL-8, and IL-1β.
source: Treatment with the single agent, ivacaftor, currently approved for patients with gating mutations, such as G551D, has also been reported to reduce sputum levels of neutrophil elastase, IL-8, and IL-1β (VX08-770-102 Study Group et al., 2011; Hisert et al., 2017), and these changes may reflect improved clinical health rather than a direct anti-inflammatory consequence of increased CFTR function.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Changes in sputum inflammatory markers with ivacaftor may reflect improved clinical health rather than a direct anti-inflammatory consequence of increased CFTR function.
source: Treatment with the single agent, ivacaftor, currently approved for patients with gating mutations, such as G551D, has also been reported to reduce sputum levels of neutrophil elastase, IL-8, and IL-1β (VX08-770-102 Study Group et al., 2011; Hisert et al., 2017), and these changes may reflect improved clinical health rather than a direct anti-inflammatory consequence of increased CFTR function.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of prior findings

claim: Monocytes isolated from clinically stable 'drug-naïve' CF patients homozygous for Phe508del have increased secretion of IL-18 and IL-1β when compared to healthy control monocytes.
source: We have previously established that monocytes isolated from clinically stable 'drug-naïve' CF patients (homozygous for Phe508del) have an increased secretion of IL-18 and IL-1β when compared to healthy control (HC) monocytes.
evidence: Supported by prior work from the authors

claim: The increased IL-18 and IL-1β response in CF monocytes was attenuated in vitro with the addition of inhibitors targeting components of the NLRP3-inflammasome or the ENaC.
source: This response was attenuated in vitro with the addition of inhibitors either targeting components of the NLRP3-inflammasome or the ENaC (Scambler et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: In vitro pre-administration of IVA/LUM for 24 hr to CF monocytes in culture halved the seven-fold rise in IL-18 observed in their absence (p<0.0001).
source: In vitro pre-administration of IVA/LUM for 24 hr to CF monocytes in culture halved the seven-fold rise in IL-18 observed in their absence (p<0.0001, for responses to stimulation with LPS-ATP, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: IVA/LUM did not attenuate the near six-fold rise in LPS-ATP-stimulated IL-1β levels in CF monocytes (p=0.9434).
source: In complete contrast, there was no drug-induced attenuation of the near six-fold rise in LPS-ATP-stimulated IL-1β levels (p=0.9434, Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: HC cells showed a two-fold elevation in cytokines after exposure to LPS-ATP alone, and IVA/LUM could not attenuate this small rise.
source: Although HC cells showed a two-fold elevation in cytokines after exposure to LPS-ATP alone, IVA/LUM could not attenuate this small rise (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B

claim: In vitro pre-administration of IVA/TEZ for 24 hr significantly reduced the post-stimulus increments in both IL-18 (p<0.0001) and IL-1β levels (p=0.0001) in monocytes of patients with CF.
source: Also, in marked contrast, the in vitro pre-administration of the other drug combination, IVA/TEZ, for 24 hr, significantly reduced the post-stimulus increments in both IL-18 (p<0.0001, Figure 1C) and IL-1β levels (p=0.0001, Figure 1D), in monocytes of patients with CF.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D

claim: IVA/TEZ had no discernable reductive effect on monocytes from HC volunteers in the presence/absence of LPS and ATP.
source: IVA/TEZ also had no discernable reductive effect on monocytes from HC volunteers in the presence/absence of LPS and ATP (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D

claim: All patients receiving IVA/LUM or IVA/TEZ therapies met the criteria for the UK compassionate use program with ppFEV1 of less than 40.
source: All patients receiving these therapies met the criteria for the UK compassionate use program, that is reflective of their percent predicted forced expiratory volume (ppFEV1) of less than 40 (HC values are typically greater than 80).
evidence: Description of patient cohort characteristics

claim: Patients received a pre-emptive course of intravenous antibiotics prior to starting treatment to ensure maximal clinical stability.
source: To ensure maximal clinical stability, patients received a pre-emptive course of intravenous antibiotics prior to starting treatment.
evidence: Description of study protocol

claim: Over the three month study period there were no significant differences in CRP, ppFEV1, FVC, WBC, neutrophil count, weight or BMI in either IVA/LUM or IVA/TEZ group.
source: Over this three month study period there were no significant differences in C-reactive protein (CRP), ppFEV1, forced vital capacity (ppFVC), white blood count (WBC), neutrophil count, weight (kg) or body mass index (BMI) in either group (Supplementary file 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for IVA/LUM; Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for IVA/TEZ).
evidence: Supported by clinical data shown in supplementary figures

claim: Serum IL-18 was significantly reduced at three months compared to baseline for IVA/LUM (p<0.0001).
source: There was a significant reduction in serum IL-18 levels, following three month's treatment with either IVA/LUM (p<0.0001, Figure 2A) or IVA/TEZ (p<0.0001, Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Serum IL-18 was significantly reduced at three months compared to baseline for IVA/TEZ (p<0.0001).
source: There was a significant reduction in serum IL-18 levels, following three month's treatment with either IVA/LUM (p<0.0001, Figure 2A) or IVA/TEZ (p<0.0001, Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The net effect of IVA/LUM and IVA/TEZ treatment was a final IL-18 cytokine level lower than the CF upper limit for both groups.
source: The net effect was a final IL-18 cytokine level lower than the CF upper limit for both groups.
evidence: Inferred from data shown in Figure 2A and 2E

claim: Values bordering on the upper limit of HC values for IL-18 were mainly seen after IVA/TEZ treatment.
source: Interestingly, values bordering on the upper limit of HC values were mainly seen after IVA/TEZ.
evidence: Inferred from data shown in Figure 2E

claim: There was no decline in serum IL-1β levels after three months therapy with IVA/LUM.
source: There was no decline in serum IL-1β levels after three months therapy with IVA/LUM (Figure 2B), and yet IVA/TEZ treatment resulted in a highly significant reduction in serum IL-1β (p=0.0009, Figure 2F; compare 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: IVA/TEZ treatment resulted in a highly significant reduction in serum IL-1β (p=0.0009).
source: There was no decline in serum IL-1β levels after three months therapy with IVA/LUM (Figure 2B), and yet IVA/TEZ treatment resulted in a highly significant reduction in serum IL-1β (p=0.0009, Figure 2F; compare 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Both IVA/LUM and IVA/TEZ treatment groups showed a significant reduction in serum TNF (IVA/LUM, p=0.0004; IVA/TEZ, p=0.0224).
source: This differential response was mirrored with the NLRP3-inflammasome-independent cytokines which, in both treatment groups, showed a significant reduction in serum TNF (IVA/LUM, p=0.0004, Figure 2C; IVA/TEZ, p=0.0224, Figure 2G) but no change in serum IL-6 levels (Figure 2D and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and 2G

claim: There was no change in serum IL-6 levels with IVA/LUM or IVA/TEZ treatment.
source: This differential response was mirrored with the NLRP3-inflammasome-independent cytokines which, in both treatment groups, showed a significant reduction in serum TNF (IVA/LUM, p=0.0004, Figure 2C; IVA/TEZ, p=0.0224, Figure 2G) but no change in serum IL-6 levels (Figure 2D and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2H

claim: There were fast and slow responders at one-month post-therapy for each cytokine, but the individual therapy response for each cytokine was different, and no correlation between individuals was observed at this time point.
source: We observed that there were fast (<25% decrease from baseline) and slow responders (<10% decrease from baseline) at one-month post-therapy for each cytokine; however, the individual therapy response for each cytokine was different, and no correlation between individuals was observed at this time point.
evidence: Inferred from data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: IVA/LUM therapy at three months revealed a broad range of effectiveness for IL-18 (109–19%) and TNF (135–18%).
source: Although IVA/LUM therapy significantly decreased IL-18 and TNF levels in serum (Figure 2A,C), the percentage to baseline response at three months revealed a broad range of effectiveness (IL-18; 109–19%; TNF 135–18%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,C), whereas for IVA/TEZ therapy, at three months, the minimum percentage decrease from baseline was 25% for IL-18, IL-1β and TNF cytokine measurements (IL-18 75–29%; IL-1β 74–33% and TNF 68–19%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, E–G) suggesting that overall, the therapy response to IVA/TEZ is more consistent across this patient group.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,C

claim: For IVA/TEZ therapy at three months, the minimum percentage decrease from baseline was 25% for IL-18, IL-1β and TNF cytokine measurements.
source: Although IVA/LUM therapy significantly decreased IL-18 and TNF levels in serum (Figure 2A,C), the percentage to baseline response at three months revealed a broad range of effectiveness (IL-18; 109–19%; TNF 135–18%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,C), whereas for IVA/TEZ therapy, at three months, the minimum percentage decrease from baseline was 25% for IL-18, IL-1β and TNF cytokine measurements (IL-18 75–29%; IL-1β 74–33% and TNF 68–19%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, E–G) suggesting that overall, the therapy response to IVA/TEZ is more consistent across this patient group.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E-G

claim: The therapy response to IVA/TEZ is more consistent across this patient group compared to IVA/LUM.
source: Although IVA/LUM therapy significantly decreased IL-18 and TNF levels in serum (Figure 2A,C), the percentage to baseline response at three months revealed a broad range of effectiveness (IL-18; 109–19%; TNF 135–18%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,C), whereas for IVA/TEZ therapy, at three months, the minimum percentage decrease from baseline was 25% for IL-18, IL-1β and TNF cytokine measurements (IL-18 75–29%; IL-1β 74–33% and TNF 68–19%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, E–G) suggesting that overall, the therapy response to IVA/TEZ is more consistent across this patient group.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Unstimulated PBMC cytokine levels generally ranged below 50 pg/ml, irrespective of exposure to either of the two drug combinations.
source: Generally, levels ranged below 50 pg/ml, irrespective of exposure to either of the two drug combinations.
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 2

claim: There were no significant changes in the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-18, IL-1β, TNF, IL-6 and IL-10 secretion by unstimulated PBMCs at baseline, or at one or three months of treatment in patients receiving either IVA/LUM or IVA/TEZ.
source: There were no significant changes in the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-18, IL-1β, TNF, IL-6 and IL-10 secretion by unstimulated PBMCs, at baseline, or at one or three months of treatment in patients receiving either IVA/LUM or IVA/TEZ (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 2

claim: At baseline (pre-therapy), LPS-ATP stimulated PBMCs secreted between ten-and fifty-fold greater amounts of IL-18, IL-1β, TNF, IL-6 and IL-10 compared to unstimulated levels.
source: Next, we stimulated the baseline CF-PBMC's with LPS and ATP. Prior to starting IVA/LUM or IVA/TEZ, at baseline (pre-therapy), the LPS-ATP stimulated PBMCs secreted between ten-and fifty- fold greater amounts of IL-18 (IVA/LUM, 642 pg/mL; IVA/TEZ, 719 pg/mL), IL-1β (IVA/LUM 1422 pg/mL; IVA/TEZ 1119 pg/mL), TNF (IVA/LUM, 517 pg/mL; IVA/TEZ, 568 pg/mL), IL-6 (IVA/LUM, 156 pg/mL; IVA/TEZ, IL-6 (217 pg/mL) and IL-10 (IVA/LUM, 37 pg/ml; IVA/TEZ 47 pg/ml).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Baseline values for LPS-ATP stimulated PBMCs are consistent with the mean values from a larger, clinically stable drug-naïve patient group.
source: These baseline values are consistent with the mean values from a larger, clinically stable drug-naïve patient group (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, E–I).
evidence: Supported by comparison with data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: After three months of IVA/LUM treatment, LPS-ATP stimulated PBMC secretion of IL-18 was significantly reduced by approximately three-fold compared to baseline (247 pg/mL p =< 0.0001).
source: After three months of patient treatment with oral therapy combinations, LPS-ATP stimulated PBMC secretion of IL-18 was significantly reduced (by approximately three-fold), compared to baseline, for both IVA/LUM (247 pg/mL p =< 0.0001, Figure 3A) and IVA/TEZ (247 pg/mL p=0.0002, Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: After three months of IVA/TEZ treatment, LPS-ATP stimulated PBMC secretion of IL-18 was significantly reduced by approximately three-fold compared to baseline (247 pg/mL p=0.0002).
source: After three months of patient treatment with oral therapy combinations, LPS-ATP stimulated PBMC secretion of IL-18 was significantly reduced (by approximately three-fold), compared to baseline, for both IVA/LUM (247 pg/mL p =< 0.0001, Figure 3A) and IVA/TEZ (247 pg/mL p=0.0002, Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: After PBMC stimulation, IL-1β remained unchanged in cells exposed in vivo to IVA/LUM.
source: Interestingly, and similar to the serum cytokine profiles, after PBMC stimulation, IL-1β remained unchanged in cells exposed in vivo to IVA/LUM (Figure 3B) after PBMC stimulation, but fell significantly in those patients receiving IVA/TEZ (378 pg/mL, p<0.0001, Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: After PBMC stimulation, IL-1β fell significantly in those patients receiving IVA/TEZ (378 pg/mL, p<0.0001).
source: Interestingly, and similar to the serum cytokine profiles, after PBMC stimulation, IL-1β remained unchanged in cells exposed in vivo to IVA/LUM (Figure 3B) after PBMC stimulation, but fell significantly in those patients receiving IVA/TEZ (378 pg/mL, p<0.0001, Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Following oral treatment, stimulated PBMC TNF secretion was significantly reduced at three months compared to baseline for both IVA/LUM (217 pg/mL p=0.0005) and IVA/TEZ (193 pg/mL, p=0.001).
source: Following oral treatment, stimulated PBMC TNF secretion was also significantly reduced at three months, compared to baseline, for both IVA/LUM (217 pg/mL p=0.0005, Figure 3C) and IVA/TEZ (193 pg/mL, p=0.001, Figure 3H) but IL-6 levels remained unchanged for both drug combinations (Figure 3D and I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3H

claim: IL-6 levels remained unchanged for both IVA/LUM and IVA/TEZ drug combinations in stimulated PBMCs.
source: Following oral treatment, stimulated PBMC TNF secretion was also significantly reduced at three months, compared to baseline, for both IVA/LUM (217 pg/mL p=0.0005, Figure 3C) and IVA/TEZ (193 pg/mL, p=0.001, Figure 3H) but IL-6 levels remained unchanged for both drug combinations (Figure 3D and I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3I

claim: Levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 significantly increased at three months post-stimulation compared to baseline for both IVA/LUM (95 pg/mL, p<0.0001) and IVA/TEZ (112 pg/mL, p=0.025).
source: Interestingly, levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 significantly increased at three months, post-stimulation, compared to baseline, for both IVA/LUM (95 pg/mL, p<0.0001, Figure 3E); and IVA/TEZ (112 pg/mL, p=0.025, Figure 3J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3J

claim: LPS-ATP-stimulation of PBMCs following IVA/LUM therapy at three months produced a minimum percentage decrease from baseline of 31% for IL-18.
source: However, in contrast to the serum cytokine profiles which showed a broad range of effectiveness for IL-18, LPS-ATP-stimulation of PBMCs following IVA/LUM therapy at three months, was found to produce a minimum percentage decrease from baseline of 31% for IL-18 but TNF remained similar to the response observed in serum (IL-18 59–22%; TNF 119–16%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C

claim: LPS-ATP-stimulated PBMCs post IVA/TEZ therapy mirrored the cytokine profiles observed at three-months in serum, with the minimum percentage decrease from baseline of 29% for IL-18, IL-1β and TNF cytokines measurements.
source: Interestingly, LPS-ATP-stimulated PBMCs, post IVA/TEZ therapy, mirrored the cytokine profiles observed at three-months in serum, with the minimum percentage decrease from baseline of 29% for IL-18, IL-1β and TNF cytokines measurements (IL-18 69–20%; IL-1β 71–8% and TNF 67–19%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-H
